meta.title: Who really said "The more I learn about people, the more I like my dog"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Mark Twain — it is French, and it is older than he is. 'Plus je connais les hommes, mieux j'aime les chiens' is in print anonymously by 1822; Lamartine is credited with a politicians' version by 1850. Twain was credited by 1911, a year after he died.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The more I learn about people, the more I like my dog'?
meta.ogDescription: An anonymous French saying in print by 1822 — thirteen years before Twain was born. He was credited with it in a Kansas newspaper in 1911, one year after his death.

answer.label: An anonymous French saying, in print by 1822
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · earliest located instance 1822, in French
answer.sourceLine: The saying is French, anonymous, and thirteen years older than Mark Twain. It appears unsigned in Tablettes Historiques et Littéraires in 1822: ‘plus je connais les hommes, mieux j’aime les chiens.’ The naturalist Alphonse Toussenel published a version in 1847, and in 1850 Count Alfred D’Orsay credited a sharper, political variant to the poet Alphonse de Lamartine. Twain, who was born in 1835 and died in 1910, was first credited with it in a 1911 Kansas newspaper — a year after his death.

source.excerpt: Plus je connais les hommes, mieux j'aime les chiens.
trail: The earliest located instance is 1822, in the French periodical Tablettes Historiques et Littéraires, and it carries no author’s name — it is already being printed as a saying rather than as somebody’s line the citation trail ↗.

It gathers famous names as it travels. Alphonse Toussenel puts a version in L’Esprit des Bêtes in 1847. In 1850 Count Alfred D’Orsay writes that Lamartine said a pointed variant about politicians: ‘Plus je vois des représentants du peuple, plus j’aime mes chiens’ — the more I see of the people’s representatives, the more I love my dogs. Lamartine stayed attached to it through French periodicals in the 1860s and 1870s. Thomas Carlyle has also been credited, in a 1923 grocery trade journal, with no support.

The Twain credit shows up in the La Cygne Weekly Record of Kansas in 1911. Searches of the sourced Twain collections turn up nothing, in English or in translation — and Twain could not have coined a saying that was in print thirteen years before he was born.
source.excerptNote: The 1822 wording, in French and unsigned. Read literally it is 'the more I know men, the better I love dogs' — a comparison of two kinds of acquaintance. The English version most people quote adds a possessive: my dog. That small change turns a general misanthropy into something warmer and much more shareable.

source.rightsNote: Free to reproduce. The saying is anonymous and in print by 1822, and every named claimant — Toussenel, D’Orsay, Lamartine (d. 1869), Carlyle, Twain (d. 1910) — has been dead well over a century, so no version is under copyright anywhere. Translations are the only wrinkle: a recent scholarly translation of the French is its own copyrightable work, but the plain rendering used here is too short and too obvious to carry rights of its own. Quote it freely; just do not put Twain’s name under it. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Mark Twain
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Twain
author.bio: Mark Twain genuinely did prefer dogs to people in print, which is why this one is so sticky. In Following the Equator (1897) he wrote, in Pudd’nhead Wilson’s New Calendar, that if you pick up a starving dog and make him prosperous he will not bite you — and that this is the principal difference between a dog and a man. That is real, sourced, and public domain, and it is a better line than the one on this page. If you want Twain being rude about humanity on behalf of dogs, quote that instead; it has the advantage of being his.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: The arithmetic does the work here. The saying was in print in 1822; Twain was born in 1835. Everything after that is a question of which famous name it collected next.

items.why: The saying is in print in French thirteen years before he was born, and no version appears in any sourced Twain collection. The earliest Twain credit located is the La Cygne Weekly Record, Kansas, 1911 — one year after his death the trail ↗.

Count D’Orsay credited him in 1850, and the credit stuck through French periodicals for decades. Two catches: it comes to us through someone else’s letter, and Lamartine’s version is about politicians, not people in general — which is a joke with a target rather than a shrug at humanity.

items.who: Published a version, did not coin it
items.why: His L’Esprit des Bêtes carries the sentiment in 1847, twenty-five years after the anonymous printing. He is a transmitter, not an origin.
A 1923 grocery trade journal claimed Carlyle coined it out of a hatred of humanity. Nothing supports it, and by 1923 the saying had already been circulating for a century.

misattribution.truthLine: An anonymous French saying, in print by 1822 — thirteen years before Mark Twain was born. He was first credited with it in 1911, the year after he died the source ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is misanthropy you are allowed to say out loud. Declaring that people disappoint you sounds bitter; routing it through a dog makes it affectionate, and the listener nods instead of worrying about you. That laundering is the whole trick, and it is why the line has survived two centuries and at least two languages.

It also holds up because the comparison is honest about what it values: not intelligence or conversation, but the absence of calculation. The dog is not better company, it is simply incapable of the specific let-down the speaker has in mind.
context.detailsSummary: Two hundred years of borrowed credit
detailsBody: 1822: printed anonymously in Tablettes Historiques et Littéraires — the earliest located instance.
1835: Mark Twain is born, thirteen years after the saying is already in print.
1847: Alphonse Toussenel publishes a version in L’Esprit des Bêtes.
1850: Count Alfred D’Orsay credits Lamartine with the politicians’ variant.
1860s–1870s: French periodicals keep the Lamartine credit alive.
1911: the La Cygne Weekly Record, Kansas, credits Mark Twain — a year after his death.
1923: a grocery trade journal credits Thomas Carlyle, with no support.
context.pull: It was in print in 1822. Twain was born in 1835.
